habitat: Singly or in small flocks, females predominating, in dry thornveld, sandveld with sparse vegetation, and grassland with scattered thorn bushes. It parasitises the Violet-eared Waxbill.
summary: A common near-endemic resident. The breeding male has a red bill and red legs, is black above and buff below, and has thin tail shafts with broadened ends. The female and non-breeding male have less distinctive head markings than other whydahs. The voice is 'chit-chit-chit', and the male has a scratchy song. Newman's size line is unreadable, so no length is stored. The Kemp name Shafttailed Whydah and the code RB were left unchanged.

similar.note: The Pin-tailed Whydah is pied, and its female has bolder head stripes.

tail.shape: Very long thin shafts with broadened ends.

head.pattern: Less distinctive head markings than other whydahs. The non-breeding male is similar.

viewNotes.note: Black above, buff below, with a red bill and thin tail shafts.
Head markings less distinctive than other whydahs.
Flight plumage is not described apart from the long tail shafts.
The underside in flight is not described.

calls.description: 'chit-chit-chit'. The male also has a scratchy song like an indigobird. The grade A call is from near Klerksdorp. The filename is XC622267-5 Good ST Whydah.mp3.

research.note: Newman calls it a common near-endemic resident, and Avibase does not mark it rare, so all twelve months are listed. The size line on the page is unreadable, so no length is stored and the error text is not copied. The grade A call is from the North West. The Kemp name Shafttailed Whydah and the code RB were left unchanged.
